# Obama's Former Physician Voices Concerns Over Health Care Reform Plan

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- President Obama frequently speaks of the mounting opposition to his health care plan. Yet one particular critic has remained conspicuously quiet throughout the debate—until now.

Dr. David Scheiner, a Chicago-based physician who served as President Obama's personal doctor for 22 years, has closely examined the president's approach to health care reform and finds it wanting.

"This isn't the kind of health care program that I think is going to work," Scheiner said.

What lends particular weight to Scheiner's critique? Beyond his decades-long relationship with the president, Scheiner voted for his former patient in the 2008 election. Yet he believes the current proposal falls short of what's truly needed. In his view, the plan's most significant flaw is that "private insurers continue to be a part of the health scheme."

*Watch Scheiner discuss his objections »*

"Everybody keeps saying we don't want the government involved in health care," Scheiner explained in an interview. "But the government is involved in Medicare, and it works."

Scheiner advocates instead for a single-payer system, similar to those in Canada and across Europe. Under this model, a single entity—potentially a government-run agency—would finance all health care costs billed by doctors, hospitals, and other providers. Proponents argue this approach would significantly reduce administrative overhead, generating substantial savings for patients.

Notably, this was a position the president himself once championed. As a rising state senator six years ago, Obama stated: "I happen to be a proponent of a single-payer universal health care plan... But as all of you know, we may not get there immediately, because first we've got to take back the White House, and we've got to take back the Senate, and we've got to take back the House."

His stance shifted during the campaign, however. "If I were designing a system from scratch, then I'd probably set up a single-payer system. But the problem is we're not starting from scratch," Obama said in Albuquerque, New Mexico, in August 2008.

Today, the president instead supports offering Americans the choice of a government-run plan that would operate alongside, and compete with, private insurers.

*Watch more on the health care debate »*

"Nobody is talking about some government takeover of health care. I'm tired of hearing that," Obama asserted in Raleigh, North Carolina, this past Thursday.

Scheiner counters that the lack of concrete details surrounding this public option makes it a difficult sell. "We don't even fully know what the public option is going to be," he said. "If the public option is too good, patients who are sick will flock to it, and I'm not sure it will be able to support itself."

Scheiner nearly had the opportunity to raise these concerns directly with the president. Though invited to a recent televised town hall meeting with Obama, he says he was ultimately dropped from the program.

"I just hope that the Congress, the American public, and the president will hear some of my words," he said. "We've got to do something better."

Scheiner finally got his chance to speak out on Thursday, joining fellow physicians who support a single-payer system in Washington to meet with lawmakers and rally public support.

He may no longer serve as the president's doctor, but Scheiner insists he's simply trying to save the patient before it's too late.

*CNN's Ed Hornick and Brittany Cummings contributed to this report.*

**Obama's Former Doctor Breaks Silence on Health Care Reform Doubts**

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- President Obama frequently references the numerous opponents rallying against his health care initiative. Yet one particular skeptic has largely stayed quiet during this ongoing debate—until now.

Dr. David Scheiner served as President Obama's personal physician for over two decades. This Chicago-based physician has carefully examined the president's health care reform strategy and found it lacking. "This program, as designed, isn't going to accomplish what needs to be done," he stated.

What gives Scheiner's opinion particular weight? For 22 years, he served as Obama's personal doctor, and he cast his vote for the Illinois senator during the 2008 presidential race.

According to Scheiner, the president's proposal simply doesn't push hard enough for real change. He identifies the plan's biggest flaw as its continued reliance on private insurance companies within the overall health care structure.

"People constantly claim they don't want government involvement in health care," Scheiner explained during an interview. "Yet Medicare is government-run, and it functions effectively."

Instead, Scheiner advocates for America to embrace a single-payer model similar to systems used in Canada and various European nations. Under this framework, one centralized payer—potentially a government agency—covers all medical expenses submitted by physicians, hospitals, and other health care providers. Supporters argue this approach eliminates costly administrative overhead, translating into substantial savings for patients.

Interestingly, this concept isn't foreign to Obama himself. Six years ago, as a rising state senator, he expressed support for exactly this kind of system. "I happen to be a proponent of a single-payer universal health care plan," Obama remarked in 2003, though he acknowledged practical political obstacles: "We may not get there immediately, because first we've got to take back the White House, and we've got to take back the Senate, and we've got to take back the House."

His stance shifted throughout the campaign trail, however. Speaking in Albuquerque, New Mexico in August 2008, he noted: "If I were designing a system from scratch, then I'd probably set up a single-payer system. But the problem is we're not starting from scratch."

Currently, Obama supports a different approach—offering Americans a government-administered plan option that would operate alongside and compete with private insurance providers. "Nobody is talking about some government takeover of health care. I'm tired of hearing that," he insisted during a Thursday appearance in Raleigh, North Carolina.

Scheiner counters that the specifics of this public option remain undefined, making it difficult to evaluate or defend. "We don't even fully know what the public option is going to be," he said. "If the public option is too good, patients who are sick will flock to it, and I'm not sure it will be able to support itself."

The physician nearly got a direct opportunity to voice his concerns to the president. Originally scheduled to participate in a televised town hall event with Obama, Scheiner claims he was ultimately removed from the lineup. "I just hope that the Congress, the American public and the president will hear some of my words," he expressed. "We've got to do something better."

Thursday finally gave Scheiner his platform. He joined fellow physicians who back single-payer reform for a gathering in Washington, where they met with legislators and energized supporters of their cause.

Though no longer treating the president personally, Scheiner sees himself as working to rescue the larger patient—the nation's health care system—before time runs out.

*CNN's Ed Hornick and Brittany Cummings contributed to this report.*

# The President's Own Doctor Speaks Out on Health Care Reform

In an unexpected twist that has drawn considerable attention, Dr. David Scheiner—who served as President Barack Obama's personal physician for 22 years—has publicly voiced his disagreement with the health care reform plan championed by his former patient. Given his close, long-standing relationship with the president, Scheiner's criticism carries a unique weight and has added an intriguing dimension to the ongoing national debate over health care policy.

At the heart of Scheiner's critique is his belief that the current reform plan simply doesn't go far enough in addressing the fundamental problems within the American health care system. He has been particularly vocal in his criticism of the continued central role that private insurance companies play under the proposed reforms. According to Scheiner, allowing private insurers to remain deeply embedded in the system undermines the potential for truly comprehensive and equitable health care coverage.

Instead, Scheiner advocates for a single-payer system, similar to the models successfully implemented in Canada and various European countries. He points to the American Medicare program—a government-run system serving seniors—as evidence that such an approach can work effectively within the United States itself. In his view, if Medicare can provide reliable coverage for millions of elderly Americans, a similar government-administered model could be expanded to serve the entire population, potentially reducing administrative costs and eliminating the profit-driven motives that he believes complicate and compromise private insurance coverage.

Adding a layer of political irony to his critique, Scheiner has highlighted the fact that Obama himself once expressed support for exactly this kind of single-payer, universal health care system. Back in 2003, while serving as an Illinois state senator, Obama spoke favorably about the concept of a single-payer approach, suggesting that he once viewed it as an ideal solution to the nation's health care challenges.

However, Obama's stance evidently shifted as he transitioned into national politics and eventually the presidency. During his presidential campaign, he acknowledged the tension between policy idealism and political pragmatism, explaining that while a single-payer system might indeed be the most logical solution if the health care system were being built from scratch, the entrenched realities of American politics—including the powerful influence of the insurance industry and the practical challenges of dismantling an existing system—necessitated a more moderate, incremental approach.

This evolution in Obama's position, from his early support for single-payer health care to his eventual embrace of a more market-based reform that preserves a role for private insurers, illustrates the broader tension between progressive policy ideals and the pragmatic compromises often required to achieve legislative success in Washington.
